showNotes: George's answer to “what bothers you most about the legal profession?” takes one word: mediocrity. Lawyers mailing it in, from the solo down the street to the AmLaw 50 firm that still gets the client's name wrong in the deal documents.

Jordan and George get into where it comes from: “File > Save As” and the copy-paste habit (and the pleading Jordan never forgot), a billable-hour model that pays for time instead of results, a bar so low that returning a phone call puts you in the top 10%, and what AI does to all of it when it's treated like a slot machine.

Then the practical part: what young lawyers who want more than mediocrity can do about it, how clients can tell when they're getting mailed-in work, why “it depends” is only the start of an answer, and how to use AI to check your lawyer without running up your bill.

chapters.title: Mediocrity, and lawyers mailing it in
Advice for lawyers who want more
Using AI to check your lawyer

showNotes: George and Jordan open with an announcement: as of five minutes ago, Campbell Teague is an “AI native” firm. Then they take the label apart. Calling yourself AI native, George says, is like being a pencil-native firm in the 1930s, and Jordan suspects it usually means “we bought a ChatGPT subscription.”

From there: why “nobody got fired for hiring the biggest firm” is losing its pull, how much of today's “AI” is workflow automation that has existed for a decade, what real adoption might look like (think Jarvis, not a chat window), and why senior lawyers who can dictate may be the surprise winners.

They close on the fate of junior lawyers, the return on delegation, what the old courthouse runners can teach us, and two spicy predictions: a slopocalypse in the courts, and the end of class action waivers.

chapters.title: The “biggest firm I could find” excuse
What real AI adoption looks like
Nobody can dictate like a boomer lawyer
